newsitem.title: USA: More firms default in high-flying wireless phone sale. [CORRECTED]
newsitem.headline: More firms default in high-flying wireless phone sale. [CORRECTED]

text.p: Nine more winners in a recent high-flying government auction of new wireless phone licenses defaulted on payments, regulators said Thursday, a further sign that some winners are struggling to raise money.
But the default rate was far less than predicted by some analysts.

One of the companies -- Carolina PCS 1 L.P. of Shelby, N.C. -- was the ninth highest of the 89 original winners in the Federal Communications Commission's sale of permits to offer a new generation of cellular phones.
It won nine licenses worth $92.7 million. The auction, which ended in May, was reserved for smaller companies.

The FCC said eight smaller winners -- the high bidders on a total of 22 licenses worth $38.1 million -- also defaulted on the second of two payments to the agency, each equal to 5 percent of a company's total bid. Payments were due Tuesday.
In May, two other companies defaulted on the initial 5 percent downpayment and the FCC re-auctioned the licenses.

The "C-Block" auction of personal communications services (PCS) licenses raised an eye-popping $10.2 billion. The price tag spurred analysts to warn that some winners would fail to raise the financing needed to proceed.
But predictions by industry officials and analysts that as many as half of the winners would default on their FCC payments have not been realised.

PCS backers promise to turn the wireless phone into a mass-market product, allowing consumers to access different communications services -- such as phone, paging, fax and Internet access -- through one hand-held device.

The other eight companies which defaulted were: Longstreet Communication International, Holmdel, N.J.; MFRI Inc., Stroudsburg, Pa.; Mountain Solutions Ltd., Lakewood, Colo.; National Telecom PCS Inc., Stamford, Conn.; RFW Inc., New York, N.Y.; Roberts-Roberts & Associates, St. Louis; Southern Communications Systems Inc., Memphis, Tenn. (corrects company from Southern Wireless, Hilton Head, S.C.); and Wireless Telecommunications Co., Scottsbluff, Neb.
Three companies -- who ultimately did make the payments but were late -- asked the FCC to waive the payment rules. Up to now, the FCC has taken a hard stance on such requests.

The nine companies follow two other winning bidders who defaulted on the initial 5 percent FCC payment. One of the companies was the No. 4 bidder in the auction, BDPCS Inc. of Portola Valley, Calif. The FCC denied the two waiver requests.
An FCC spokeswoman said the agency would act on the latest requests "as soon as possible."

The defaults are more evidence some winners are finding it tough to scrape up financing amid scepticism among potential lenders over the profitability of PCS. Analysts say there are too many companies wanting to get into the business.
Two of the top winners in the C-Block auction -- No. 1 NextWave Telecom Inc. and No. 3 General Wireless Inc. -- have faced hurdles on Wall Street in raising funds, analysts said.
